summary: This Wikipedia article describes bicycle performance as measurable factors such as energy efficiency, speed, weight, and power requirements that affect how effective a bicycle is. It covers mechanical efficiency of drivetrains, the energy comparison between cycling and walking, human power output limits, typical and record speeds, the effects of reducing weight and rotating mass, and the power needed to overcome air drag, rolling resistance, climbing and acceleration. The text shown is truncated partway through the climbing power section.
one_line: Wikipedia article on bicycle performance: the energy efficiency, speeds, weight effects, and power requirements that determine how effective a bicycle is.
key_facts: Cycling is calculated to be the most efficient self-powered means of transportation in terms of energy a person must expend to travel a given distance.
Up to 99% of mechanical energy delivered by the rider into the pedals is transmitted to the wheels (clean, lubricated new chain at 400 W).
Gearing mechanisms reduce transmitted energy by 1–7% for clean derailleurs and a straight chainline, 4–12% for chain with 3-speed hubs, and 10–20% for shaft drive with 3-speed hubs.
A human at 70 kg requires about 60 watts to walk at 5 km/h on firm flat ground, while the same person on an ordinary bicycle travels at 15 km/h with the same power output.
The energy expenditure of cycling is about one-third that of walking the same distance under those conditions.
Active humans can produce 1.5 W/kg (untrained), 3.0 W/kg (fit), and 6.6 W/kg (top-class male athletes).
Maximum sustained power over one hour ranges from about 200 W (NASA experimental group of healthy men) to 500 W (men's world hour record).
For cyclists in Copenhagen, the average cycling speed is 15.5 km/h (9.6 mph).
The highest speed officially recorded for a human-powered vehicle on level ground is 144.18 km/h (89.59 mph), set in 2016 by Todd Reichert in the Eta Speedbike, a streamlined recumbent bicycle.

The highest speed officially recorded for an upright conventional bicycle under fully faired conditions was 82 km/h (51 mph) over 200 m, set in 1986 by Jim Glover on a Moulton AM7 at Expo86 in Vancouver.
The fastest bicycle speed in slipstream is 296 km/h (183.9 mph), set by Denise Mueller-Korenek in 2018 on the Bonneville Salt Flats, slipstreaming behind a dragster.
The UCI sets a minimum bicycle weight limit of 6.8 kg for sanctioned races.
A 10% reduction of total system weight (bicycle, rider, and luggage) will save nearly 10% of power when climbing steeply.
For a 90 kg rider and bike in a flat criterium at 40 km/h, a 10% mass reduction could give about a 3% advantage.
Air drag power is initially very low and increases with the cube of speed, and the drag coefficient CD is roughly approximated as 1 for usual cycling speeds on an upright bicycle.
Rolling resistance coefficients measured on a roller mechanism are 0.003 to 0.006 at low speed for tires inflated to maximum recommended pressure, increasing about 50% at 10 m/s.
